terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs a query file against a fresh copy of the bakehouse database.

tasks.title: List the cafes in Port Ellery
tasks.description:
Odile is planning the Port Ellery round and needs every cafe in that town with its email address.

In `queries/1-port-ellery-cafes.sql`, write one `SELECT` that returns exactly two columns:

- `name`: the cafe's name
- `email`: the cafe's `contact_email`, renamed

Include only cafes whose `town` is `Port Ellery`, sorted by name from A to Z. Keep cafes without an email: they show `NULL`.

The check runs your file on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset with different cafes, and compares the rows, the column names and the order.
nextSteps: Run `node run.mjs queries/1-port-ellery-cafes.sql` and read the message it prints.
Write `SELECT * FROM cafes;` first to see every column and value.
Choose the two columns, rename the email column and filter by town.
Add the sort and run the file again.
hints: Text values in SQL go in single quotes, and the comparison is exact, including capital letters.
`AS` gives a column a new name in the result without changing the table.
The query has four parts in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY. ORDER BY sorts from A to Z unless you say otherwise.

tasks.title: Pick products for the counter display
tasks.description:
Tobias wants a list for the new counter display: cheap sweet things, plus every rye product, because rye is what the bakehouse is known for.

In `queries/2-shelf-picks.sql`, return the columns `name`, `category` and `price` for every product that is either:

- in the category `pastry` or `cake` and priced under 3.00, or
- has `rye` anywhere in its name, in any category and at any price

Use `IN` for the categories and `LIKE` for the name. Row order does not matter. The check compares your rows with the expected rows on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset.
nextSteps: Write the first condition on its own and run it.
Write the rye condition on its own and run it.
Join the two with OR, using parentheses so each half means what you intend.
Check that a 4.65 rye loaf and a 2.60 bun both appear.
hints: `category IN ('a', 'b')` is a short way to write two equality checks joined by OR.
In LIKE, `%` matches any run of characters, so put it on both sides of the word. In SQLite, LIKE ignores the case of plain letters.
AND binds tighter than OR. Wrap the category and price conditions in parentheses together, then OR the name condition.

tasks.title: Find the newest cafes with no email
tasks.description:
Invoices go out by email, and some cafes never gave one. Odile will phone the most recent ones first.

In `queries/3-missing-emails.sql`, return `name`, `town` and `joined_on` for cafes whose `contact_email` is missing (`NULL`). Sort them by `joined_on` with the newest first, and return only the first 5.

The check compares rows and their order on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset.
nextSteps: List every cafe with its email and spot the ones that show NULL.
Sort newest first, then keep the first 5 rows.
hints: NULL means no value at all, so it is never equal to anything, not even to NULL.
SQL has a special test for missing values: `IS NULL`. `= NULL` returns no rows.
Dates stored as YYYY-MM-DD text sort correctly as text. Add DESC after the column in ORDER BY, then LIMIT 5 at the very end.
